newsitem.title: USA: Jurors who think Simpson murdered wife join pool.
newsitem.headline: Jurors who think Simpson murdered wife join pool.

text.p: Three people who said they thought O.J. Simpson probably murdered his ex-wife and her friend were added on Tuesday to the pool of jurors retained for further questioning in the former football star's civil trial.

So far in the first phase of jury selection in which panellists were asked what they knew of Simpson's criminal trial, 19 of 61 jurors selected to advance to the second phase of questioning said they believed Simpson guilty based on that trial.

Simpson was acquitted by a criminal jury a year ago this week of the June 12, 1994, murders of Niciole Brown and Ronald Goldman. He is being sued in a civil lawsuit by the victims' families who want him found responsible for the killings.

Among those who told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki and lawyers for both sides on Tuesday that they believed Simpson was probably guilty was a black man about 40 who said he believed Simpson's blood was at the crime scene, "but how it got there is certainly debatable."

The man, the first black man questioned in the civil trial to say he thought Simpson was probably guilty, also criticised the Los Angeles police for its investigation of the murders and the handling of crucial blood evidence. "They made mistakes, they weren't perfect," he said.

Fujisaki, over the strong objections of Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, also accepted a potential juror, a white man in his 30s, who said the DNA evidence presented against Simpson in the criminal trial was "compelling," that there was no evidence of any other suspects and that Simpson was "violent and hit his wife on many occasions."
Baker argued that to have such a juror on the panel would shift the burden of proof from the plaintiffs' attorneys to the defence, which was "not fair and not the law."
Fujisaki described the prospective juror as "marginal" but said he would retain him for further questioning.

A white man in his sixties said he initially felt sympathy for Simpson when he learned of his arrest, but came to think he had probably committed the murders after he fled his home in a famous slow-speed police chase.

The other two prospective jurors retained for further questioning during Tuesday morning's session were a white woman and a black woman, both of whom said they had not followed the criminal trial closely and had no opinions on Simpson's guilt or innocence.
